messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

We are trying to develop a hierarchical model to fit a specific kind of data. We thought that some existing function in unmarked might do the work but until now we have not been able to do that.
Here it is as our data look like. We have a number of sites (i) that are surveyed by multiple observers (j) over a number of sessions (t). At least for the moment we want to assume that the superpopulation size (M) of individuals susceptible of being available in a certain site is constant among sessions, Mi~Poisson(λ). However the number of individuals available to be detected at each session can change throughout the t sessions so that Nit~Binomial(Mi,φit). We need to account for the possibility that φ changes over time t and space i. For several reasons we cannot use the classical robust design approach with secondary occasions so we think we may estimate the detection probability by using multiple observers at each session t. In some sense the secondary occasions would be replaced by multiple observers. So, by calling y the number of counted individuals would be:  yijt~Binomial(Nit,pit). In other words we would be assuming that the detection probability p does not vary as a function of the observer j but uniquely as a function of time t and space i.

Our parameter of main interest is f. We want to investigate how this parameter changes across sites and over time.

Is there any existing function in unmarked that might be accommodated to fit this data type?
We tried with gmultmix but it seems to us that, even if it includes the possibility of multiple observers, it always requires secondary occasions.
Any help would be really appreciated.
Best,

Simone

messages.subject: Infinite confidence intervals with predict
messages.body_plain:
Hello, I am hoping to use gdistsamp to estimate density at different sites based on repeated point counts, and also compare density of multiple species.  But since my dataset is large and messy, I am starting with smaller subsets and simulations to try to figure things out.  I have found the examples and discussions here very helpful, thank you!  Could someone help me understand why the predict function sometimes returns what appears to be good estimates but with huge confidence intervals (approaching infinity or maximum possible range)?

For example, suppose some sites have no detections, because of unsuitable habitat, and a site covariate 1/0 explains suitable (1) vs. unsuitable (0).  The abundance prediction for the unsuitable sites tends to be near 0, with low SE, but with huge CI (0 to infinity).  I guess this is because abundance can’t be less than 0, so it is unable to generate a CI around 0?  But should the SE be OK even though the CI is not?  If I “cheat” by adding a single detection, I get a reasonable CI (e.g., 0.00 to 0.02).  Is there any other solution?  Assuming that phi is the same across all sites, wouldn’t it make sense to want to predict close to 0 abundance at sites with unsuitable habitat, expecting a narrower CI for a species with higher phi, wider CI for a species with lower phi?

Just to be very clear, I re-created this scenario using the example simulation for gdistsamp for transects (http://www.inside-r.org/packages/cran/unmarked/docs/gdistsamp).  I copied the simulated data (umf) to a spreadsheet, added 50 more sites all with 0 detections, and a dummy site covariate 0/1 (1 for the original 50 sites with simulated detections, and 0 for the additional 50 sites with no detections).  I read the new CSV (changing the # transects to 100), and ‘predict’ again returned infinite CI for sites with covariate 0 (but reasonable CI if I add just a single detection):
m1 <- gdistsamp(~dummy, ~1, ~1, umf, output="density", K=1000)
newdat <- data.frame(dummy=c(0,1))
predict(m1, type="lambda", newdata=newdat)

Thanks for any insights or suggestions,
Ed

 this is almost surely a result of the low information (poor precision) with which the parameters are estimated for your model.  This is a very basic statistical issue in any model -- if parameters are poorly estimated then so are predictions or other derived quantities.  If you simulate with larger data sets under which parameters are well estimated then you shouldn't have any problems.

 I am working on ungulate data from Colombian Guiana forest with Royle y Nichols approach. We developed the sampling in two protected area, one with continue Amazon forest and the second with Riparian forest. We make 15 lineal transect about 3 to 5 km by long, detecting species (tracks, direct observation) during consecutive days in April and July of the same year.

 But, reading the new Book of Kery & Royle, maybe it better include this random factor in a Bayesian approach.

 I appreciate any opinion on the best way to go ahead and any advice to a valid approach to include the spatial relations between spatial subunits by transect (block)?

Thanks in advance,

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] RN model with spatial subunits along line transects
messages.body_plain:
Dear Bibiana,

in your design there is a basic nested structure with three levels like this:
section / transect / area

What we wrote in the new book in the section on multiscale occupancy models is that we emphasize that such nested designs have a long history in experimental design, where the associated analyses are usually called split plots or nested analysis of variance. The modern way to analyze such data is with mixed models, where, in your case, you would specify random transect effects that are nested within each area, in addition probably to an area effect. Such an analysis would take account of possible non-independence of the units of your analysis, which are the transect sections and get the SEs right etc.

Now in capture-recapture, occupancy and related models which are mostly used for strictly observational data, people are not so much used to seeing such hierarchies and hence, often such nested blocking structures are ignored. Moreover, an occupancy or an Nmix model is already quite complex to fit compared to simple ANOVAs and traditional mixed models, and the standard software such as unmarked, PRESENCE and MARK cannot deal with additional sets of random effects (beyond the random site effects)

When you ignore such dependencies in the data induced by such nesting, then according to the traditional wisdom you will be too liberal: i.e., get too narrow CIs and too low p-values. I think that you could analyse your data with unmarked using the RN model, provided that you acknowledge this. The advantage is that you don't need to learn BUGS and you can use significance testing or AIC model selection, all of which is less straightforward when you go bayesian.

Note that you may potentially have another type of dependency in your data, that along the same transect, where your measurements for neighbouring segments may not be independent, but rather be spatially autocorrelated. See Tiger on Trail paper by Jim Hines et al.

Wonder what others say about these issues of non-independence ?

Best regards to Colombia from Marc

messages.subject: Re: Power analysis - comparing methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi Brent,

As you've read, for a power analysis you need to simulate data under certain conditions and fit models to see how well you are able to estimate parameters of interest.  If you've got R code for an occupancy-based power analysis, adapting it to your questions involves selecting a range of sampling conditions, estimating occupancy and/or covariate relationships under multiple (e.g., >100) data replicates, and calculating RMSE or some other metric of accuracy. Dear Ainars,

Your idea is one that comes up repeatedly: why not use spatial replicates for N-mixture-model-type abundance estimation in a similar way as spatial replicates are often used instead of temporal replicates in occupancy models ?

However, in general I think that this cannot be done: normally, the “closure” assumption will not be met in such cases, because spatial replicate locations will have a different abundance. Interestingly, in your case where the traps are so close one could make the closure assumption if it were not for the fact that the individuals are removed from the population, which again changes N and hence represents a violation of closure.

Had your traps been “strung out” in time over a short period of closure, you could use a multinomial N-mixture model with removal design, but due to simultaneous trap deployment, you can’t do this either.

So I think you’re limited to modeling relative abundance using some sort of Poisson GLMM.

Best regards  -- Marc

I have a dataset of carabid beetle collected in farmland using pitfall traps. The sampling design consists of 80 random sites with (up to) 4 traps each. I wonder if these pseudo-replicates (traps) can be treated as "visits" in pcount() model? I understand that these are not true replicates in time and those beetles that fall into one trap are not "available for catching" in the other traps thus resulting in lower lambda estimate. However, I am mainly interested in differences among sites and impact of site covariates and not so much in the true abundance or detection probability per se. Do you see any other problems with using the pcount() and treating the traps as visits? Any suggestions?

Dear Ainars,

Your idea is one that comes up repeatedly: why not use spatial replicates for N-mixture-model-type abundance estimation in a similar way as spatial replicates are often used instead of temporal replicates in occupancy models ?

However, in general I think that this cannot be done: normally, the “closure” assumption will not be met in such cases, because spatial replicate locations will have a different abundance. Interestingly, in your case where the traps are so close one could make the closure assumption if it were not for the fact that the individuals are removed from the population, which again changes N and hence represents a violation of closure.

Had your traps been “strung out” in time over a short period of closure, you could use a multinomial N-mixture model with removal design, but due to simultaneous trap deployment, you can’t do this either.

So I think you’re limited to modeling relative abundance using some sort of Poisson GLMM.

Best regards  -- Marc
